rail.role: Web development — sole owner; worked closely with co-designer (PR Manager)

index.title: MALTALINK — conference registration flow redesign
index.summary: I replaced a scattered register-then-chase-payment flow with one checkout. One stakeholder told me the comparison wasn't worth running — I ran it anyway.

headline: Payment and registration in one step — every purchaser registered.

hero.alt: Ticket Tailor checkout at the Details step: payer fields with an Event and attendee details section beneath them, under a Tickets–Details–Payment breadcrumb.

problem: The 2024 conference ran registration and payment through two disconnected systems: Eventbrite for payment, and a separate Google Form — more than ten sections long, with no field validation — for attendee details. The only link between them was a ticket buyer manually copying their Eventbrite order ID into a free-text field on the form. Planning data was unreliable throughout — even the Eventbrite listing itself carried conflicting dates. The new team's purpose for 2025 was straightforward: improve the registration experience.
constraint: Phased deadlines across 4-5 months, with registration, finance, and volunteering teams each holding requirements. One senior stakeholder favored the fast path — tools already familiar and licensed — and time pressure made pragmatic shortcuts tempting throughout.
decision: One stakeholder with real influence said further research wasn't worth doing. I ran a focused comparison anyway — respectfully — and brought a live demo instead of an argument. Side by side, Astra + Ticket Tailor won on flexibility, richer registration forms, centralized PDF/CSV export, automatic QR-code check-in, and far lower ongoing fees. The demo, not my opinion, moved the decision — and registration became one step inside a single, validated checkout — replacing the hand-typed order ID that had been the only link between 2024's two disconnected systems.

figures.alt: The 2024 Google Form's required Eventbrite Order ID field, next to the Eventbrite listing's own contradiction: a 'Sales ended Mon, May 13 - 9 AM' claim sitting above an agenda showing a full Saturday, 9 AM to 7 PM.
Ticket Tailor invoice for the conference: 200 ticket credits at 0.42 each, 84.00 EUR total, nothing due.

evidence.caption: The Google Form's only link to payment was a hand-typed Eventbrite order ID — no validation, easy to mistype or skip. The Eventbrite listing itself couldn't agree with its own agenda on when the conference even ran.

result.label: RESULT
result.body: Every ticket purchaser completed registration — the mandatory checkout step made drop-off structurally impossible. Launched November 2025 and ran without downtime through the conference; the post-conference survey rated registration and website 4.55/5. Recognition followed: an official certificate of appreciation, a public LinkedIn recommendation citing ownership, vision, and a crash-free launch, and an invitation into the Website Manager role for 2026.

lesson: Sometimes the person with influence will tell you research isn't worth doing. Run it anyway, respectfully, and let the side-by-side make the case. Compromise on the day-to-day; hold firm with evidence on the few calls that matter.
